lit-real-02-c1.quote: The French novelist Honoré de Balzac (1799-1850) was the first writer to use fiction to convey the total social scene prevailing within one country at a particular period in its history.
lit-real-02-c1.claim: Honoré de Balzac (1799-1850) was the foundational French realist.

lit-real-02-c3.quote: The novel gained notoriety after the French government charged Flaubert with obscenity and stopped its publication, determining the work to be a challenge to moral decency.
lit-real-02-c3.claim: The famous trial that followed publication, the French government prosecuted Flaubert for offending public morals, established the novel's reputation.

lit-real-03-c4.quote: Ivan Turgenev (1818–1883): A Russian novelist, best known for Fathers and Sons (1862), which illustrates the divide between generations.
lit-real-03-c4.claim: His Fathers and Sons (1862) is the canonical novel of generational conflict.

lit-real-05-c2.quote: Émile Zola (1840-1902) was the foremost proponent of the doctrine of naturalism in literature.
lit-real-05-c2.claim: Émile Zola (1840-1902) was naturalism's central figure.

lit-real-05-c2.quote: and with much courage and recklessness of consequences Zola challenged the findings of the court-martial in an open letter to the President of the Republic (J'accuse, Jan. 13, 1898).
lit-real-05-c2.claim: Zola also wrote 'J'Accuse...!' (1898), the open letter that broke open the Dreyfus Affair.

lit-real-01-c3.text: Erich Auerbach (1946). Mimesis Epilogue. We Refugees Archive.
lit-real-01-c3.quote: the book was written during the war and at Istanbul, where the libraries are not well equipped for European studies.
lit-real-01-c3.claim: Erich Auerbach wrote Mimesis: The Representation of Reality in Western Literature (1946) in wartime Istanbul exile

lit-real-04-c2.quote: Of the novels of the 1880s The Rise of Silas Lapham (1885) is the most famous.
lit-real-04-c2.claim: Major novels: The Rise of Silas Lapham (1885)
